about: THE IRISH SEA WORLD, 780-1070: the Irish kingdoms, Dal Riata and the Picts (from about 900 Alba), Norse Dublin, Man and the Isles. Who rules, the wars, the raids, the laws, the coins and the church, so the game can say who holds the Liffey, Iona and the sea between in any year and what that means for a small ship. Realm ids in ports_793.json: 'irish' (port duiblinn), 'dalriata' (port hi); legacaestir (Chester, realm mercia) is the English door on this sea and is named where the event is there. Every ruler has 'part': tara (the king of Tara, the over-king of the Ui Neill, called king of Ireland by the annals from the 9th century), leinster (the province Dublin lies on the edge of), munster (the kings of Cashel, and from 978 Brian's house), dublin (the Norse kings of Ath Cliath, 853-1070), dalriata (the Gaelic kingdom of Argyll, to about 843), picts (the kings of Fortriu, to 900), alba (from 900), isles (Man and the Hebrides: thinly recorded), orkney (the earls, overlords of the Isles at times: saga dates only). To ask who rules a place in a year, take the entries of that place's part whose from-to holds the year; duiblinn before 841 and 902-917 is under leinster and tara; hi is dalriata to about 843, then picts/alba in name and the Isles' Norse lords in fact. Years are whole years AD; days are in the text. 'seat' and 'where' are port ids from ports_793.json where the place is one, else a plain place name. 'certainty' is sure / likely / uncertain, as in chronicle_793.json; 'chronicle' gives the id of the matching entry there, where there is one. 'by_realm' true marks a raid made out of this realm on others. IMPORTANT: this file was written from the writer's knowledge of the annals and the standard works without re-reading each entry on the web; annal entry numbers (AU 851.3) are given where remembered and are otherwise left as the year. (?) marks a doubt. The lists of Leinster and Munster kings between the well-known names, the Isles, and all Orkney dates are the weakest parts. No words are quoted from any modern translation: everything is retold in plain words. Written 6 October 2026. Edit freely.

abbreviations.AU: Annals of Ulster, by year and entry (ed. Mac Airt and Mac Niocaill 1983; CELT, celt.ucc.ie)

abbreviations.AClon: Annals of Clonmacnoise (an English version of 1627)
abbreviations.FA: Fragmentary Annals of Ireland (11th-century saga-like annals: use with care)
abbreviations.Cogadh: Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh, The War of the Irish with the Foreigners (early 12th century, written to praise Brian's house)
abbreviations.CKA: Chronicle of the Kings of Alba (10th century, in the Poppleton manuscript)
abbreviations.ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, with the manuscript letter and the annal year
abbreviations.JW: John of Worcester, Chronicle, by year
abbreviations.HR: Historia regum (ascribed to Symeon of Durham)

the coins and hoards themselves, with the standard work named

rulers.name: Donnchad Midi mac Domnaill
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Died on 6 February 797 (?), an old man, after twenty-seven years.

rulers.name: Aed Oirdnide mac Neill
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Won the kingship in battle at Druim Rig (797). The first king of Tara said to be ordained by a churchman, hence his by-name. Died in 819 at Ath da Ferta.

rulers.name: Conchobar mac Donnchada
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Died in 833 after a reign troubled by Feidlimid of Munster and by the first great raids.

rulers.name: Niall Caille mac Aeda
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Beat the heathens at Derry (833) and Mag Itha (845) and Feidlimid at Mag nOchtair (841). Drowned in 846 in the river Callan near Armagh.

rulers.name: Mael Sechnaill mac Maele Ruanaid
rulers.title: king of Tara; called king of all Ireland at his death
rulers.how_ended: Drowned Turgeis (845), killed seven hundred heathens at Forach (848), plundered Dublin (849), took hostages of Munster (854-858). Died on 30 November 862.

rulers.name: Aed Findliath mac Neill
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Cleared the Norse forts off the north coast (866) and won at Cell Ua nDaigri (868). Died on 20 November 879 at Druim Inasclainn.

rulers.name: Flann Sinna mac Maele Sechnaill
rulers.title: king of Tara; called king of Ireland on the cross at Clonmacnoise
rulers.how_ended: Beaten by the Dublin Norse in 888; killed Cormac of Cashel at Belach Mugna (908). Died on 25 May 916.

rulers.name: Niall Glundub mac Aeda
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Held the fair of Tailtiu again (916), marched against the new fleets (917), and was killed with twelve kings by Sitriuc's men at Islandbridge by Dublin in mid-September 919.

rulers.name: Donnchad Donn mac Flainn
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Burned Dublin (936) and besieged it (938). Died in 944.

rulers.name: Congalach Cnogba mac Maele Mithig
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Sacked Dublin (944) and killed Blacaire (948). Ambushed and killed in 956 by the Dublin Norse and the Leinstermen at Tech Guigrann on the Liffey.

rulers.name: Domnall ua Neill
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Died in penance at Armagh in 980, the year of the battle of Tara.

rulers.name: Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill (first reign)
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Won at Tara (980), took Dublin three times (980, 989, 995). Gave Brian the south in 997 and yielded the kingship to him in 1002 without a battle.

rulers.name: Brian Boruma mac Cennetig
rulers.title: king of Ireland; written 'emperor of the Irish' in the Book of Armagh (1005)
rulers.how_ended: Killed in his tent at Clontarf on Good Friday, 23 April 1014, as his army won. Buried at Armagh.

rulers.name: Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill (second reign)
rulers.title: king of Tara
rulers.how_ended: Burned the suburbs of Dublin (1015). Died on 2 September 1022 on Cro Inis in Lough Ennell. After him no king was agreed by all.

rulers.name: Donnchad mac Briain
rulers.title: king of Munster, claiming Ireland (a king with opposition)
rulers.how_ended: Never held the north. Worn down by Diarmait of Leinster and his own nephew Toirdelbach; put out in 1063, went to Rome and died there in 1064.
rulers.note: No king of Tara is agreed for 1022-1072; the game should name the strongest king, not a high king.

rulers.name: Diarmait mac Mael na mBo
rulers.title: king of Leinster and of the Foreigners, the strongest king in Ireland (a king with opposition)
rulers.how_ended: Killed in battle at Odba on 7 February 1072 by Conchobar ua Mael Sechnaill of Mide.

rulers.name: Ruaidri mac Faelain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Died in 785.

rulers.name: Bran Ardchenn mac Muiredaig
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Burned in a house with his queen Eithne, daughter of the king of Tara, on 6 May 795 by Finsnechta.

rulers.name: Finsnechta Cethardec mac Cellaig
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Submitted to Aed in 804, was put out in 805 (the province shared between two Muiredachs), came back in 806 and died at Kildare in 808.

rulers.name: Muiredach mac Ruadrach and Muiredach mac Brain
rulers.title: kings of Leinster (shared)
rulers.how_ended: The son of Bran died in 818, the son of Ruaidri in 829.

rulers.name: Cellach mac Brain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Fought the community of Kildare in 833 and killed many of them. Died in 834.

rulers.name: Bran mac Faelain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Set up by Niall Caille in 835. Died in 838.

rulers.name: Lorcan mac Cellaig
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: With Olchobar of Munster killed twelve hundred Northmen and the jarl Tomrair at Sciath Nechtain in 848. His end is not recorded (?).

rulers.name: Tuathal mac Maele Brigte
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed by his own kin in 854 (?).

rulers.name: Ruarc mac Brain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 862 (?).

rulers.name: Muirecan mac Diarmata
rulers.title: king of Naas and of eastern Liffey
rulers.how_ended: Killed by Northmen in 863.

rulers.name: Dunlaing mac Muiredaig
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Died in 869.

rulers.name: Ailill mac Dunlainge
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed by Northmen in 871.

rulers.name: Domnall mac Muirecain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed by his own companions in 884.

rulers.name: Muiredach mac Brain
rulers.title: king of Leinster and abbot of Kildare
rulers.how_ended: Died in 885.

rulers.name: Cerball mac Muirecain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: With the men of Brega drove the Norse out of Dublin in 902; fought at Belach Mugna (908). Died of a wound in 909.

rulers.name: Augaire mac Ailella
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed with many lords and a bishop by Sitriuc's fleet at Cenn Fuait (Confey) in 917.

rulers.name: Faelan mac Muiredaig
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Taken captive by the Dublin Norse in 925 and let go. Died in 942.

rulers.name: Lorcan mac Faelain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed by the Norse while raiding Dublin in 943.

rulers.name: Broen mac Maelmorda
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Sacked Dublin with Congalach in 944. Killed raiding Osraige in 947.

rulers.name: Tuathal mac Augaire
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Died in 958. The Ui Tuathail (O'Toole) are named from him.

rulers.name: Cellach mac Faelain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Died in 966.

rulers.name: Murchad mac Finn
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed by treachery by Domnall Cloen in 972.

rulers.name: Augaire mac Tuathail
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed by the Dublin Norse at the battle of Bithlann (Belan) in 978.

rulers.name: Domnall Cloen mac Lorcain
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Held prisoner in Dublin in 979 and freed by Mael Sechnaill after Tara (980). Killed in 984.

rulers.name: Donnchad mac Domnaill Cloen
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Taken by Sitriuc of Dublin in 999; put out by Brian in 1003 in favour of Mael Morda.

rulers.name: Mael Morda mac Murchada
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Brother of Gormlaith, uncle of Sitriuc of Dublin. Rose against Brian in 1013 and was killed at Clontarf on 23 April 1014.

rulers.name: Dunlaing mac Tuathail, then Donncuan mac Dunlainge
rulers.title: kings of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Dunlaing died in 1014; Donncuan was killed in 1016.

rulers.name: Bran mac Maelmorda
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Blinded in Dublin in 1018 by Sitriuc, his cousin, by treachery. The Ui Brain (O'Byrne) are named from him.

rulers.name: Augaire mac Dunlainge
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Beat Sitriuc at Delgany in 1021. Killed in 1024.

rulers.name: Donnchad mac Dunlainge
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Blinded in 1036 by Donnchad of Osraige, who had taken the province in 1033 (?).

rulers.name: Donnchad mac Gilla Patraic
rulers.title: king of Osraige and of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Held the fair of Carman in 1033 on taking Leinster. Died in 1039.

rulers.name: Murchad mac Dunlainge
rulers.title: king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 1042 in battle with Osraige; the last Ui Dunlainge king of the province.

rulers.name: Diarmait mac Mael na mBo
rulers.title: king of Leinster; from 1052 king of the Foreigners too
rulers.how_ended: Took Dublin in 1052; sheltered Harold Godwinson (1051-1052) and Harold's sons (1066-1069). Killed at Odba on 7 February 1072.

rulers.name: Olchobar mac Flainn (?)
rulers.title: king of Munster (also called abbot of Inis Cathaig)
rulers.how_ended: Died in 796 (?). Artri was ordained in 793, so the two overlap or the lists are wrong.

rulers.name: Artri mac Cathail
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Ordained king in 793. Died in 821.

rulers.name: Feidlimid mac Crimthainn
rulers.title: king of Munster, also bishop and scribe
rulers.how_ended: Burned and seized great churches (Clonmacnoise 833, Kildare 836), camped at Tara (840), was beaten by Niall in 841. Died on 28 August 847, called the best of the Irish, a scribe and anchorite.

rulers.name: Olchobar mac Cinaeda
rulers.title: king of Munster (and abbot of Emly)
rulers.how_ended: Won at Sciath Nechtain (848). Died in 851.

rulers.name: Ailgenan mac Donngaile
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Died in 853.

rulers.name: Mael Gualae mac Donngaile
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Gave hostages to Mael Sechnaill. Taken by the Northmen in 859 and stoned to death.

rulers.name: Cenn Faelad ua Mugthigirn
rulers.title: king of Munster (and abbot of Emly)
rulers.how_ended: Died in 872.

rulers.name: Dunchad mac Duib da Bairenn
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Died in 888.

rulers.name: Dub Lachtna mac Maele Gualae
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Died in 895.

rulers.name: Finguine Cenn nGecan mac Loegairi
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Put out in 901 and killed by his own people in 902.

rulers.name: Cormac mac Cuilennain
rulers.title: king of Munster and bishop
rulers.how_ended: The scholar-king, to whom the word-book Sanas Cormaic is ascribed. Killed at Belach Mugna on 13 September 908 fighting Flann Sinna and Leinster; his head was brought to Flann.

rulers.name: Flaithbertach mac Inmainen
rulers.title: king of Munster, abbot of Inis Cathaig
rulers.how_ended: Gave up the kingship for the pilgrim's staff about 922; died in 944.

rulers.name: Lorcan mac Coinligain
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: End not recorded (?).

rulers.name: Cellachan Caisil mac Buadachain
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Carried off as a hostage by Muirchertach of the Leather Cloaks in 941. Died in 954. The saga of his wars with the Norse (Caithreim Chellachain) is 12th-century praise, not history.

rulers.name: Mael Fathardaig, Dub da Bairenn, Fer Graid, Donnchad mac Cellachain
rulers.title: kings of Munster (four short reigns)
rulers.how_ended: 957, 959 (killed), 961 (killed), 963: the last Eoganacht kings of weight.

rulers.name: Mathgamain mac Cennetig
rulers.title: king of Munster (Dal Cais)
rulers.how_ended: Beat the Limerick Norse at Sulchoit and sacked Limerick (967). Seized by treachery in 976 and killed by Mael Muad.

rulers.name: Mael Muad mac Brain
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Killed by Brian at Belach Lechta in 978.

rulers.name: Brian Boruma mac Cennetig
rulers.title: king of Munster; from 1002 king of Ireland
rulers.how_ended: Killed at Clontarf, 23 April 1014.

rulers.name: Dungal ua Donnchada
rulers.title: king of Cashel
rulers.how_ended: Died in 1025; the sons of Brian fought each other meanwhile (Tadc murdered 1023).

rulers.name: Donnchad mac Briain
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Put out in 1063; died a pilgrim at Rome in 1064.

rulers.name: Toirdelbach ua Briain
rulers.title: king of Munster
rulers.how_ended: Diarmait's man until 1072, then the strongest king in Ireland and lord of Dublin. Died in 1086.

rulers.name: The abbots of Duiblinn (no king)
rulers.title: a church by the black pool, with the ford Ath Cliath upstream; the land is the Ui Dunlainge kings' of Leinster, Brega begins across the Liffey
rulers.how_ended: The heathens made a ship-fort at Duiblinn in 841 and wintered.
rulers.source: AU 790 (the death of an abbot of Duiblinn (?)); AU 841.4

rulers.name: The fleet at Duiblinn (no named king)
rulers.title: chiefs of the ship-fort
rulers.how_ended: Plundered by Mael Sechnaill (849), slaughtered by the dark heathens (851), and submitted to Amlaib in 853. Turgeis (drowned 845) is not said by the annals to have ruled Dublin.

rulers.name: Amlaib (Olaf), 'son of the king of Laithlind'
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Took the submission of the Foreigners and tribute from the Irish (853). Last seen in Ireland in 871; killed in Pictland by Constantine about 874 (?).

rulers.name: Imar (Ivar)
rulers.title: king of the Northmen of all Ireland and Britain (at his death)
rulers.how_ended: Ruled with Amlaib. Died in 873, of sickness by one account (?). His grandsons, the Ui Imair, held Dublin, York, Waterford, Limerick and the Isles for two hundred years.

rulers.name: Auisle (Asl)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners, with his brothers
rulers.how_ended: Killed by his own kin in 867.

rulers.name: Oistin mac Amlaib (Eystein)
rulers.title: king of the Northmen
rulers.how_ended: Killed by treachery by Albann (Halfdan) in 875.

rulers.name: Albann (Halfdan)
rulers.title: king of the dark heathens, claiming Dublin
rulers.how_ended: Killed in a sea-fight with the fair heathens on Strangford Lough in 877.

rulers.name: Barid mac Imair
rulers.title: king of the Northmen
rulers.how_ended: Raided Saint Cianan's church at Duleek and died in Dublin in 881: killed and burned by the saint's power, the annals say.

rulers.name: The son of Auisle (name lost)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners (?)
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 883 by Otir son of Iergne and Muirgel, daughter of Mael Sechnaill.

rulers.name: Sichfrith mac Imair
rulers.title: king of the Northmen
rulers.how_ended: Killed by treachery by his kinsman in 888.

rulers.name: Sitriuc mac Imair
rulers.title: king of the Northmen
rulers.how_ended: The town split in 893 between him and Sichfrith the jarl. Killed by other Northmen in 896.

rulers.name: Imar ua Imair
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Driven out with all the Foreigners in 902. Killed by the men of Fortriu in 904.

rulers.name: No Norse king: the fort stands empty
rulers.title: the kings of Brega and Leinster hold the Liffey
rulers.how_ended: Sitriuc grandson of Imar came back with a fleet in 917.

rulers.name: Sitriuc Caech (Sihtric) ua Imair
rulers.title: king of the fair and dark Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Won at Cenn Fuait (917) and Islandbridge (919). Left Dublin in 920 for York; married King Aethelstan's sister in 926 and died in 927.

rulers.name: Gofraid ua Imair (Guthfrith)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Plundered Armagh in November 921 but spared the prayer-houses, the Culdees and the sick. Tried York in 927 and was back within six months. Died of sickness in 934, called a most cruel king.

rulers.name: Amlaib mac Gofraid (Olaf Guthfrithson)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Broke the Limerick fleet on Lough Ree (August 937), lost at Brunanburh (937), took York in 939 and died in 941.

rulers.name: Blacaire mac Gofraid
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Killed Muirchertach of the Leather Cloaks (26 February 943); lost the town to sack in 944 and gave it up to Amlaib Cuaran in 945.

rulers.name: Amlaib Cuaran (Olaf Sihtricson) (first reign)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Baptised in England in 943 with King Edmund as sponsor. Beaten at Slane in 947 and went back to York (to 952).

rulers.name: Blacaire mac Gofraid (second reign)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Killed by Congalach in 948 with sixteen hundred killed or taken.

rulers.name: Gofraid mac Sitriuc
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Carried three thousand captives out of Kells and four other churches in 951 and died the same year, as a sickness ran through the Foreigners of Dublin.

rulers.name: Amlaib Cuaran (second reign)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Thirty years: the town grows rich. His sons lost the battle of Tara in 980; he went to Iona in penance and died there (980 or 981).

rulers.name: Gluniairn mac Amlaib (Jarnkne)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners, under his half-brother Mael Sechnaill
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 989 by his own slave when drunk.

rulers.name: Sitriuc mac Amlaib (Sihtric Silkbeard)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Put out for a year by Imar of Waterford (994-995); fled after Glenn Mama (999) and came back as Brian's man and son-in-law; stayed inside the walls at Clontarf; struck the first coins; went to Rome (1028) and founded Christ Church. Driven overseas in 1036 by Echmarcach; died in 1042.

rulers.name: Echmarcach mac Ragnaill (first reign)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Replaced by Imar son of Aralt in 1038.

rulers.name: Imar mac Arailt
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Raided Rathlin and Armagh. Driven out in 1046; died in 1054.

rulers.name: Echmarcach mac Ragnaill (second reign)
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Went over the sea when Diarmait of Leinster burned the country round and took the town in 1052. Kept Man until 1061; died a pilgrim at Rome about 1065.

rulers.name: Murchad mac Diarmata
rulers.title: king of the Foreigners under his father Diarmait, king of Leinster
rulers.how_ended: The first Irish king of Dublin. Took tribute from Man in 1061. Died in Dublin in 1070 and was buried there.

rulers.name: Fergus mac Echdach
rulers.title: king of Dal Riata
rulers.how_ended: Died in 781.

rulers.name: Donncoirce
rulers.title: king of Dal Riata
rulers.how_ended: Died in 792.

rulers.name: Conall mac Taidg
rulers.title: king in Dal Riata (earlier a king among the Picts, beaten in 789)
rulers.how_ended: Killed in Kintyre in 807 by Conall mac Aedain.

rulers.name: Conall mac Aedain
rulers.title: king of Dal Riata
rulers.how_ended: Four years, by the king-lists (?).

rulers.name: Domnall mac Caustantin
rulers.title: king of Dal Riata, son of the king of the Picts
rulers.how_ended: Twenty-four years by the lists (?). Dal Riata is by now ruled from Fortriu.
rulers.source: Duan Albanach; Synchronisms of Flann Mainistrech

rulers.name: Aed mac Boanta
rulers.title: king of Dal Riata
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 839 with the king of the Picts in the great battle against the heathens.

rulers.name: Alpin, then his son Cinaed mac Ailpin (Kenneth)
rulers.title: kings of Dal Riata (by the later lists)
rulers.how_ended: Cinaed took the Pictish kingship about 843. After him no king of Dal Riata is named; the Isles go to the Foreigners.

rulers.name: Caustantin mac Fergusa (Constantine)
rulers.title: king of Fortriu (the Picts)
rulers.how_ended: Beat Conall mac Taidg in 789. Said to have founded Dunkeld. Died in 820.

rulers.name: Oengus mac Fergusa
rulers.title: king of Fortriu
rulers.how_ended: Died in 834. Saint Andrews' founding legend names him (?).

rulers.name: Drest mac Caustantin and Talorgan mac Uuthoil
rulers.title: kings of the Picts (shared)
rulers.how_ended: Three years by the king-list.

rulers.name: Eoganan mac Oengusa
rulers.title: king of Fortriu
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 839 with his brother Bran and men past counting by the heathens.

rulers.name: Uurad mac Bargoit, then Bred and rival kings
rulers.title: kings of the Picts
rulers.how_ended: Short reigns after the disaster of 839; rivals to Cinaed are listed down to about 848.

rulers.name: Cinaed mac Ailpin (Kenneth I)
rulers.title: king of the Picts
rulers.how_ended: Raided English Lothian six times, burned Dunbar and Melrose; brought relics of Columba to Dunkeld (849). Died in February 858 at Forteviot, of a growth.

rulers.name: Domnall mac Ailpin (Donald I)
rulers.title: king of the Picts
rulers.how_ended: In his time the Gaels made the laws of Aed son of Eochaid at Forteviot. Died in April 862.

rulers.name: Causantin mac Cinaeda (Constantine I)
rulers.title: king of the Picts
rulers.how_ended: Paid hostages to Amlaib (866), saw Dumbarton fall (870), had its king Artgal killed (872). Killed by the Northmen in 876 (877 by some).

rulers.name: Aed mac Cinaeda
rulers.title: king of the Picts
rulers.how_ended: Killed by his own companions in 878.

rulers.name: Giric mac Dungail (with Eochaid son of Rhun of Strathclyde (?))
rulers.title: king of the Picts
rulers.how_ended: Later lists say he first freed the Scottish church from secular dues. Put out in 889 (?).

rulers.name: Domnall mac Causantin (Donald II)
rulers.title: king of the Picts; at his death the first called king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: The Northmen wasted Pictland in his time. Killed at Dunnottar in 900.

rulers.name: Causantin mac Aeda (Constantine II)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Killed Imar's grandson (904), swore with Bishop Cellach at Scone (906), fought Ragnall at Corbridge (918), bowed to Aethelstan (927), was invaded (934), lost a son at Brunanburh (937). Gave up the kingdom in 943 for the staff of a monk at Saint Andrews; died in 952.

rulers.name: Mael Coluim mac Domnaill (Malcolm I)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Given Cumbria by King Edmund in 945 on terms of help by land and sea. Killed by the men of the Mearns in 954.

rulers.name: Illulb mac Causantin (Indulf)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: In his time Edinburgh was left to the Scots. Killed by a fleet of Northmen at Cullen in 962.

rulers.name: Dub mac Mael Coluim
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Killed by the Scots themselves at Forres in 967.

rulers.name: Cuilen mac Illuilb
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Killed by the Britons of Strathclyde in 971, burned in a house by a man whose daughter he had taken.

rulers.name: Cinaed mac Mael Coluim (Kenneth II)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: At Chester before Edgar in 973. Killed by treachery at Fettercairn in 995.

rulers.name: Causantin mac Cuilen (Constantine III)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Killed in a battle between Scots in 997.

rulers.name: Cinaed mac Duib (Kenneth III)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Killed at Monzievaird in 1005 by Mael Coluim.

rulers.name: Mael Coluim mac Cinaeda (Malcolm II)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Beaten at Durham (1006), won at Carham (1018) and held Lothian; bowed to Cnut (about 1031). Died at Glamis on 25 November 1034.

rulers.name: Donnchad mac Crinain (Duncan I)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Beaten at Durham in 1040. Killed by his own men under Mac Bethad near Elgin on 14 August 1040, still young.

rulers.name: Mac Bethad mac Findlaich (Macbeth)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Seventeen years, mostly quiet; went to Rome in 1050 and gave silver to the poor. Beaten by Earl Siward on 27 July 1054; killed at Lumphanan on 15 August 1057.

rulers.name: Lulach mac Gilla Comgain
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Killed by Mael Coluim at Essie on 17 March 1058.

rulers.name: Mael Coluim mac Donnchada (Malcolm III)
rulers.title: king of Alba
rulers.how_ended: Raided Northumbria in 1061; took in the English exiles after 1066 and married Margaret about 1070. Killed at Alnwick in 1093.

rulers.name: No king named: Dal Riata's islands, and Man (ruled, it seems, by a British house tied to Gwynedd (?))
rulers.how_ended: Raided from 794. Merfyn Frych, king of Gwynedd from 825, is said to come from the land of Manaw (?).

rulers.name: Gofraid mac Fergusa (doubtful) and Ketill Flatnose (saga)
rulers.title: chief of the Isles of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Gofraid's death in 853 is only in AFM and may be a later invention. Ketill is the sagas' ruler of the Hebrides; he may be the Caittil the Fair beaten in Munster in 857 (?).

rulers.name: The kings of Dublin and their kin (Ui Imair)
rulers.title: overlords of Man and the Isles
rulers.how_ended: Ragnall won a sea-fight off Man in 914. No king of the Isles is named until the sons of Aralt.

rulers.name: Maccus mac Arailt
rulers.title: king of very many islands
rulers.how_ended: Raided Anglesey (971), came to Edgar at Chester (973), took Imar of Limerick off Scattery Island (974). Last heard of in 984.

rulers.name: Gofraid mac Arailt
rulers.title: king of the Isles of the Foreigners
rulers.how_ended: Raided Anglesey (972, 980, 987), won the battle of Man (987). Killed in Dal Riata in 989.

rulers.name: Ragnall mac Gofraid
rulers.title: king of the Isles
rulers.how_ended: Died in 1005. Earl Sigurd of Orkney takes tribute in the Hebrides in these years, by the sagas.

rulers.name: Sigurd of Orkney's men (Earl Gilli of the Hebrides, by the saga), then unknown
rulers.how_ended: Sigurd fell at Clontarf (1014). Who held Man from 1014 to the 1030s is not known (?).

rulers.name: Echmarcach mac Ragnaill
rulers.title: king of Man and of the Rhinns of Galloway (and twice of Dublin)
rulers.how_ended: Perhaps the Iehmarc who bowed to Cnut about 1031. Beaten in Man by Murchad of Dublin in 1061, who took tribute; died at Rome about 1065, called king of the Rhinns.

rulers.name: Murchad mac Diarmata of Dublin; then Godred son of Sitric
rulers.title: overlord of Man; king of Man
rulers.how_ended: Godred son of Sitric was king in Man in 1066 and took in Godred Crovan, a fugitive from Stamford Bridge, who won the island in 1079.

rulers.name: Sigurd Eysteinsson, 'the Mighty'
rulers.title: earl of Orkney
rulers.how_ended: Died of a scratch from the tooth of a dead enemy's head tied to his saddle, the saga says. All dates are guesses.

rulers.name: Torf-Einar Rognvaldsson
rulers.title: earl of Orkney
rulers.how_ended: Died in his bed. Named for teaching the islanders to burn peat.

rulers.name: Thorfinn Skull-splitter (after his brothers Arnkel and Erlend, who fell with Eric at Stainmore)
rulers.title: earl of Orkney
rulers.how_ended: Died in his bed about 963 (?); his sons fought over the earldom.

rulers.name: The sons of Thorfinn, last of them Hlodvir
rulers.title: earls of Orkney
rulers.how_ended: Hlodvir died about 991 (?).

rulers.name: Sigurd Hlodvisson, 'the Stout'
rulers.title: earl of Orkney, taking tribute in the Hebrides and Man
rulers.how_ended: Baptised by force by Olaf Tryggvason about 995, by the saga. Killed at Clontarf on 23 April 1014 under his raven banner.

rulers.name: Sumarlidi, Einar, Brusi and Thorfinn, sons of Sigurd
rulers.title: earls of Orkney (shared)
rulers.how_ended: Thorfinn outlived his brothers and killed his nephew Rognvald Brusason about 1046.

rulers.name: Thorfinn Sigurdarson, 'the Mighty'
rulers.title: earl of Orkney, Shetland, Caithness and the Hebrides
rulers.how_ended: Went to Rome about 1050 and set a bishop at Birsay. Died about 1065; his sons Paul and Erlend followed Harald of Norway to Stamford Bridge in 1066.

wars.who: Heathens from the north (out of western Norway by way of Shetland and Orkney) against the island churches and coasts
wars.what: Forty years of hit-and-run raids by small fleets on Iona, Skye, Rathlin or Lambay, Inishmurray, Howth, Bangor, Skellig, Armagh. No bases; the raiders go home for the winter. Local kings sometimes win (811, 812).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Island churches stop being safe stores of silver and wine. The Columban community moves its head house from Iona to Kells (807-814). A small ship in the Hebrides or the North Channel in summer is prey.

wars.who: Aed Oirdnide, king of Tara, against Leinster
wars.what: Aed wastes Leinster twice in one month (804), divides it between two kings (805), and is beaten at the Liffey (808).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Liffey plain, the land behind Duiblinn, is burned over twice. Cattle, the only money, are driven off.

wars.who: Feidlimid mac Crimthainn of Munster against the Ui Neill kings of Tara and their churches
wars.what: A bishop-king who burns church lands (Gallen 823, Clonmacnoise 833), seizes the abbot of Armagh at Kildare (836), meets Niall at Cloncurry (838), camps at Tara (840), and is beaten at Mag nOchtair (841). All this while the first big fleets arrive.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No church is safe from Christians either. The two strongest kings look at each other, not at the Liffey: the ship-fort of 841 goes up unhindered.

wars.who: Great fleets of Northmen against all Ireland
wars.what: Sixty ships on the Boyne and sixty on the Liffey (837); a fleet on Lough Neagh (839-841); ship-forts at Linn Duachaill and Duiblinn (841); Turgeis on Lough Ree (844-845) until Mael Sechnaill drowns him. In 848 the Irish kings win four battles (Forach, Sciath Nechtain, Daire Disirt Do-Chonna, Dun Maele Tuile) and send gifts and word of it to King Charles in Francia.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The raiders now stay all year and sell what they take: Duiblinn becomes a slave market and a winter harbour. Up the rivers nothing is safe; at the ship-fort a foreign trader is welcome.

wars.who: Heathens against the men of Fortriu and Dal Riata
wars.what: A battle in which the king of the Picts, his brother, the king of Dal Riata and men past counting fall.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Both royal houses of the north are wiped out in a day. Out of it comes Cinaed mac Ailpin's single kingdom; the western isles are left to the Northmen.

wars.who: Dark Foreigners (Dubgaill, Danes) against Fair Foreigners (Finngaill, the Norse already in Ireland)
wars.what: A fleet of 140 ships of the king of the Foreigners comes to make the Norse in Ireland obey (849). Dark heathens sack the ship-fort at Dublin (851) and win a three-day sea-fight on Carlingford Lough (852). In 853 Amlaib, son of the king of Laithlind, comes; all the Foreigners submit to him and the Irish pay him tribute.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Two years in which nobody knows who takes the landing-due at Dublin. From 853 there is one king there, and a king wants traders.

wars.who: Mael Sechnaill, king of Tara, against Amlaib and Imar of Dublin and Cerball of Osraige
wars.what: Great warfare (856), with the Gall-Goidil, foreign-Irish of mixed blood, fighting for hire on both sides. Amlaib and Imar raid Mide with Cerball (859). A royal meeting at Rath Aeda meic Bric (859) makes peace among the Irish and hands Osraige to the northern half.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin's king is now one player among the Irish kings, hired and married into. A merchant can be passed from one to the other.

wars.who: Amlaib, Auisle and Imar of Dublin against the Picts and the Britons of the Clyde; Aed Findliath against the Norse of the north coast
wars.what: Amlaib and Auisle plunder all Pictland and take hostages (866). While they are away Aed destroys every Norse fort on the north coast and takes twelve score heads at Lough Foyle (866); Amlaib's fort at Clondalkin is burned (867); Aed wins at Cell Ua nDaigri (868). Amlaib burns Armagh (869). Dumbarton Rock falls after four months when the well runs dry (870); two hundred ships carry English, Britons and Picts to Dublin (871).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No Norse town ever grows in the north of Ireland: the trade stays at Dublin. In 871 slaves are cheap at the Liffey as never before.

wars.who: The heirs of Imar and Amlaib against Halfdan of the dark heathens
wars.what: Imar dies (873). Halfdan, from Northumbria, slaughters the Picts (875), kills Amlaib's son by treachery (875), and is killed on Strangford Lough (877).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The start of what a later writer calls forty years' rest from new fleets (about 876-916): Dublin is weaker, quarrels with itself (893), and trades.

wars.who: Cerball of Leinster and Mael Finnia of Brega against Dublin
wars.what: The heathens are driven from Ireland, from the fort of Ath Cliath; they leave a great many ships and get away half dead. Ingimund's band tries Anglesey, is beaten off, and is given land near Chester by Aethelflaed of the Mercians.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin's market shuts for fifteen years. Its people and silver go to Man, the Wirral, the Ribble, the Isles: Chester gains what Dublin loses.

wars.who: Flann Sinna and Cerball of Leinster against Cormac of Munster
wars.what: Battle of Belach Mugna, 13 September 908: the bishop-king of Cashel is killed.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Munster is leaderless when the fleets come back to Waterford six years later.

wars.who: The grandsons of Imar (Ragnall and Sitriuc) against the Irish kings, the Scots and the English
wars.what: Ragnall wins a sea-fight off Man (914); a great new fleet settles at Waterford (914). In 917 Sitriuc camps at Cenn Fuait and kills the king of Leinster, and takes Dublin back. Ragnall fights Constantine and the English of Bamburgh at Corbridge (918) and takes York. Niall Glundub, king of Tara, attacks Dublin and is killed at Islandbridge (September 919).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin reopens under kings who also hold York: for thirty years one family taxes both ends of the road across Britain. Waterford and soon Limerick become towns too.

wars.who: Dublin against the Norse of Limerick
wars.what: Fleets on the Shannon lakes and Lough Erne; Limerick's men take Lough Ree. In August 937 Amlaib of Dublin breaks their ships there and carries off their king, then sails for England.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin makes itself the one head of the Foreigners in Ireland. The west-coast trade answers to it.

wars.who: Aethelstan, king of the English, against Constantine of Alba, Owain of the Cumbrians and Amlaib of Dublin
wars.what: Aethelstan wastes Alba by land as far as Dunnottar and by sea as far as Caithness (934). In 937 Dublin, Alba and the Cumbrians invade together and are beaten at Brunanburh: five kings and seven jarls dead; Amlaib gets back to Dublin with few.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A bad autumn at Dublin: ships lost, widows, ransom to find. Chester, the English mint facing Ireland, is at its busiest in these years.

wars.who: The kings of Tara and Ailech against Dublin
wars.what: Donnchad burns Dublin (936); a siege (938); Muirchertach of the Leather Cloaks takes a fleet to the Hebrides (941) and is killed by Blacaire at Ardee (26 February 943). Congalach and the Leinstermen sack Dublin in 944: houses, ship-sheds and all burned, the women, boys and common people carried off. Blacaire is killed in 948.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The town is now rich enough to be worth sacking by the Irish. After 944 it must be rebuilt almost from the ground.

wars.who: Edmund, king of the English, against the Cumbrians (Strathclyde)
wars.what: Edmund wastes all Cumbria and lets it to Malcolm of Alba on condition he be his helper by sea and land.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Solway and Clyde shore answers to the king of Alba.

wars.who: Dublin against Brega and the midland churches
wars.what: Gofraid takes three thousand people and much gold and silver out of Kells (951). Congalach, king of Tara, is ambushed and killed by the Dubliners (956).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The biggest slave haul in the Irish record. Then a sickness in the town (951).

wars.who: Mathgamain and Brian of the Dal Cais against the Norse of Limerick and their Irish allies
wars.what: Battle of Sulchoit and the sack of Limerick (967): the saddles, silks and silver are carried off and the captives lined up on a hill. Imar of Limerick is killed on Scattery Island (977); Brian wins Munster at Belach Lechta (978).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Limerick becomes an Irish king's town that keeps its Norse traders. The pattern for Dublin later.

wars.who: Mael Sechnaill, king of Tara, against Dublin
wars.what: Battle of Tara (980): the Dubliners and the men of the Isles are cut down. A three-day siege follows: all Irish hostages and slaves are freed, two thousand cattle paid, the Ui Neill freed of tribute. A second siege of twenty nights (989) ends with an ounce of gold on every house-plot each Christmas for ever. In 995 he takes the ring of Thor and the sword of Carlus.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin is from now on a town under an Irish over-king: it pays, and is left to trade. The slave market loses its Irish stock in a day in 980.

wars.who: Danes and the sons of Aralt in the Isles
wars.what: Three ships of Danes land in Dal Riata; seven score are hanged and the rest sold (986). Danes kill the abbot of Iona and fifteen elders on Christmas night (986). Gofraid son of Aralt and Danes win the battle of Man, a thousand dead (987); 360 of those who plundered Iona are killed (987). Gofraid is killed in Dal Riata (989).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The worst years in the Isles since the 800s. Stay south of the Mull of Kintyre.

wars.who: Brian Boruma against Leinster, Dublin, and at last their allies from Orkney and Man
wars.what: Brian and Mael Sechnaill share Ireland (997). They beat Leinster and Dublin at Glenn Mama (30 December 999) and Brian sits in Dublin from New Year to Candlemas 1000, burning the fort and Thor's wood. King over all from 1002. Leinster and Dublin rise in 1013. On Good Friday, 23 April 1014, at Clontarf Brian's army wins and Brian, his son, his grandson, the king of Leinster, Earl Sigurd of Orkney and Brodir of Man die. Dublin itself is not taken.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin loses fighting men, not its trade: Sitriuc rules another twenty-two years and the mint goes on. The Orkney earls' hold on the Isles is broken for a generation.

wars.who: Aethelred, king of the English, against Cumberland and Man
wars.what: The king wastes nearly all Cumberland; his fleet, sent round by Chester and unable to meet him, wastes Man.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A bad summer to lie at Man or in the Dee.

wars.who: Malcolm II of Alba and Owain the Bald of Strathclyde against the Northumbrians
wars.what: Battle of Carham on the Tweed, after a comet of thirty nights: the Scots win and keep Lothian.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The border of Alba comes down to the Tweed. Not an Irish Sea matter, but it makes Alba a kingdom worth an English king's notice.

wars.who: Sitriuc of Dublin against his neighbours
wars.what: Mael Sechnaill burns the suburbs (1015); Sitriuc blinds the king of Leinster (1018), is beaten at Delgany (1021) and at sea by the Ulaid (1022), raids Kells (1019) and Ardbraccan (1031); his son Amlaib is taken by the king of Brega and ransomed (1029) for 1,200 cows, 120 Welsh horses, 60 ounces of gold, 60 of silver, and the sword of Carlus.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A small, rich, quarrelsome town-kingdom. The ransom list of 1029 is the best record of what Dublin had to give: cattle, British horses, gold and silver by the ounce.

wars.who: The houses of Moray and Atholl in Alba; Earl Siward of Northumbria
wars.what: Mac Bethad kills Duncan (1040), kills Crinan of Dunkeld with 180 men (1045), is beaten by Siward (27 July 1054: 3,000 Scots and 1,500 English dead), and killed (1057); Lulach is killed (1058).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Little at sea. In Alba there is no town and no coin: a merchant deals with a mormaer's steward or an abbot.

wars.who: Diarmait mac Mael na mBo of Leinster against Echmarcach of Dublin and Man
wars.what: Diarmait burns the land of the Foreigners from the Liffey north and takes Dublin (1052); his son Murchad is king. Murchad crosses to Man in 1061, beats Echmarcach and takes tribute.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin has an Irish king for the first time and loses nothing by it: its fleet is now for hire to English exiles. One lord holds both sides of the sea for a few years.

wars.who: English exiles with Dublin ships against England
wars.what: Harold and Leofwine, Godwine's sons, winter with Diarmait (1051-1052) and come back with nine ships to Porlock. Earl Aelfgar hires eighteen ships in Ireland (1055). In 1058 a fleet under Magnus, son of the king of Norway, with men of Orkney, the Isles and Dublin, is in the Irish Sea. After Hastings Harold's sons come from Dublin against Bristol and Somerset (1068) and Devon (1069).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Dublin's chief export for twenty years is ships with crews. The Severn and Dee ports watch for them.

raids.what: All the islands of Britain laid waste: the first raid in the Irish annals.
Iona plundered for the first time; the same summer Rechru (Rathlin or Lambay) is burned and its shrines broken, and Inishmurray and Inishbofin in the west are hit.

raids.where: Inis Patraic (St Patrick's Isle off Skerries, a day north of duiblinn; or Peel in Man (?))
raids.what: The island burned, a tribute of cattle taken from the districts, the shrine of Do-Chonna broken; great raids by sea between Ireland and Alba.
Iona burned.
Sixty-eight of the community killed. The next year building begins at Kells.

raids.where: Howth (the headland north of duiblinn bay)
raids.what: Howth plundered and a great prey of women carried off: the first slave raid on the Dublin coast.
Bangor plundered, the oratory broken, the relics of Comgall shaken from their shrine (823-824). In 824 the hermit Etgal is taken from Skellig and dies of hunger and thirst.
Blathmac son of Flann is killed on Iona for refusing to say where Columba's shrine is buried. Walafrid Strabo at Reichenau made a poem of it.
raids.source: AU 825.17; Walafrid Strabo, Versus de beati Blaithmaic vita et fine

raids.what: Armagh plundered for the first time, three times in one month.
Clondalkin plundered; also Lismore, Derry is defended by Niall.

raids.who: heathens from Inber Dea (Arklow or Wicklow)
raids.what: Half the church of Kildare burned; the first prey taken from southern Brega, many killed and very many carried off.

raids.who: a fleet of sixty ships on the Liffey and sixty on the Boyne
raids.what: The two fleets plunder the plain of the Liffey and Brega, churches, forts and farms. The men of Brega win one fight; the Ui Neill lose a great one.
A ship-fort at Duiblinn, from which Leinster and the Ui Neill are plundered as far as Slieve Bloom; another at Linn Duachaill. They are still there the next year: the first wintering.
Forannan, abbot of Armagh, taken with his relics and his people and carried to the ships at Limerick. He is back the next year.

raids.who: Mael Sechnaill, king of Tara, and Tigernach of Lagore
raids.what: The Irish plunder the ship-fort.
The newcomers make a great slaughter of the fair Foreigners and plunder the ship-fort, people and goods.

raids.who: Amlaib, Imar and Auisle, with Lorcan of Mide
raids.what: The three kings of the Foreigners search the old burial caves of Brega for treasure, a thing never done before.

raids.who: Cennetig of Loigis and Mael Ciarain
raids.what: Amlaib's fort at Clondalkin burned and a hundred heads of his chief men taken.
Armagh plundered and burned with its oratories; a thousand carried off or killed.
A siege of four months; the fortress plundered and destroyed.
The army rides across England to a deserted city in the Wirral called Chester and winters; the English burn the corn round it and they go into Wales.

raids.who: the men of Brega and Leinster
raids.what: The fort of Ath Cliath taken; the Foreigners flee leaving many ships.

raids.who: Ingimund's Norse from Dublin, settled on the Wirral, with Danes and Irish
raids.what: They attack Chester; the townsmen throw down stones, boiling ale and at last beehives. A late and saga-like tale; that Aethelflaed restored Chester in 907 is sure.
Dublin taken back for the Foreigners.
Armagh entered on the Saturday before Martinmas (10 November); the prayer-houses with the Culdees and the sick are spared, and the church, but some houses burn through carelessness.
Dublin burned. (The same year Amlaib of Dublin plunders Clonmacnoise and stays two nights.)

raids.who: Congalach of Brega and Broen of Leinster
raids.what: Dublin sacked: houses, fences, ships and all buildings burned; women, boys and common people carried off; four hundred fighting men killed. Its jewels, goods and cloth taken.
Kells, Donaghpatrick, Ardbraccan, Dulane and Kilskeer plundered from one camp: three thousand people or more taken, with gold, silver, cattle and horses.
After Tara, a siege of three days and nights: every Irish hostage and slave in the town freed, two thousand cattle and jewels paid.
Cheshire much harried.
Iona plundered on Christmas night; the abbot and fifteen elders killed.
A siege of twenty nights; the townsmen drink nothing but sea water and give him what he asks: an ounce of gold from every house-plot, every Christmas night, for ever.
After Glenn Mama Brian enters Dublin about New Year, takes its gold, silver and captives, burns the fort and cuts down Thor's wood; Sitriuc flees north, finds no shelter, and comes back to submit.

raids.who: King Aethelred's fleet out of Chester
raids.what: The fleet wastes Man.

The great Gospel of Colum Cille, the chief relic of the western world for its cover, is stolen by night from the sacristy of the great stone church; found after two months and twenty nights under a sod, its gold stripped off.
The battle is fought at Clontarf across the Tolka from the town; the fort is not taken.

raids.who: Mael Sechnaill and the northern kings
raids.what: The fort's surroundings burned, all the houses outside the walls.

raids.who: Diarmait mac Mael na mBo of Leinster
raids.what: Fine Gall burned from Dublin to the Delvin; fighting round the fort; Echmarcach goes overseas and Diarmait takes the kingship.

raids.who: Murchad son of Diarmait, king of Dublin
raids.what: Murchad crosses to Man, beats the son of Ragnall and takes tribute.

raids.who: the sons of Harold with a fleet from Dublin
raids.what: They try Bristol, are beaten off by the townsmen, and fight in Somerset; they come again in 1069 with sixty-four ships to the Taw.

laws.what: The Law of Adomnan (the Law of the Innocents), sworn at Birr by the abbot of Iona and ninety-one kings and churchmen of Ireland, Dal Riata and the Picts, and renewed in 727: women, clerics and children are not to be killed, struck or taken in war; the fines go to Iona's community.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Backstory, and still the law in 793. Iona's steward collects the fines. A man who carries a woman off as a slave owes eight cumals to the saint, in a land where the unit of value is itself a slave woman.

laws.what: Standing Irish law (the law tracts of the 7th and 8th centuries): no coin. Worth is counted in the cumal (a slave woman, reckoned as three milk cows), the set, the milk cow, the ounce of silver and its twenty-fourth, the scruple. A man's honour-price sets what he may swear to, go surety for and be paid if wronged.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Prices are named in cows and ounces and paid in whatever is to hand. Every bargain needs sureties (men who pledge their own honour-price that it will be kept) and is void if made drunk, or with a slave, a son without his father, or a monk without his abbot.
laws.source: Kelly, chapters on contract, surety and units of value; Di Astud Chor

laws.what: Standing Irish law on strangers: a man from over the sea (the cu glas, grey dog) and a castaway have no honour-price of their own. They have standing only through the lord or the church that takes them in, or a wife's kin.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Before a king or abbot has named you his guest you can be robbed without a fine. Find a protector first; he will want a gift and first choice of the cargo. A king's or an abbot's protection lasts a fixed time and breaking it is paid for at his honour-price.
laws.source: Kelly, chapters on rank and on protection (snadud); Uraicecht Becc

laws.what: Standing Irish law of the sea (Muirbretha, the sea-judgments, known from fragments): what the sea throws up belongs to the owner of the shore, up to a set value, the rest to the kindred and king; a ship driven ashore is in the keeping of the lord of that shore, who must feed the crew; goods found beyond nine waves out are the finder's.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A wreck is not yours once it lies on another man's strand unless he has taken you into his protection first. The nine waves are the edge of the land's law.

laws.what: The law of the fair (oenach): each king holds a fair for his people; the king of Tara holds the Fair of Tailtiu at Lugnasad (about 1 August), Leinster the Fair of Carman, every third year (?). During the fair there is peace: no fighting, no seizing goods for debt, no carrying off. The 11th-century poem on Carman names three markets: of food, of livestock, and of the foreigners with gold and fine cloth.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The one time a stranger can sell inland in safety. Miss the days and there is no market until next year. Tailtiu fails in 811 (a church boycott), in the 870s, and lapses from 927 to 1006 except when a king revives it (916, 1006); Carman is held by whoever claims Leinster (1033).
laws.source: AU 811.2; AU 873; AU 876; AU 916; AU 1006; AU 1033; Metrical Dindshenchas, Carmun (ed. Gwynn)

laws.what: The Law of Patrick: Armagh's law protecting clerics and claiming Armagh's dues, proclaimed province by province with a king's backing: Cruachain 783, Connacht 799, by the king of Tara 806, Connacht 811 and 825, Munster 823, and again later. Rival saints have theirs: Ailbe (Munster 793), Coman (Connacht 793), Ciaran (814), Daire's law against cattle-raiding (812, 813).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: When a saint's law is proclaimed his stewards go round with his relics collecting. A trader carrying goods for a church travels under that church's law; harming him is paid for to the saint.

laws.what: The synod of the Ui Neill at Dun Cuair, led by Condmach of Armagh: clerics are freed from going on hostings.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Church tenants cannot be called out by the king. Church land is the steadier place to keep a store.

laws.what: Amlaib takes the submission of all the Foreigners in Ireland and tribute from the Irish. From now there is a king at the ship-fort of Dublin.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: One man to pay at the Liffey, and his peace on the strand. What the landing-due was is not recorded (?); in a Norse harbour of the time it would be a gift to the king's man and his first pick of the cargo.

laws.what: The royal meeting at Rath Aeda meic Bric: Mael Sechnaill, the abbots of Armagh and Clonmacnoise and the kings make peace among the men of Ireland; Osraige is handed over to the northern half.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A year of peace inland; the kings turn on Dublin together.

laws.what: The laws of Aed son of Eochaid: in Donald I's time (858-862) the Gaels and their king make the rights and laws of the kingdom of Aed (a king of Dal Riata who died in 778) at Forteviot.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: In Pictland the law is now the Gaels' law, the same in kind as Ireland's: honour-prices, sureties, no coin.

laws.what: The Law of Sunday (Cain Domnaig) comes to Ireland with a letter said to have fallen from heaven, brought by a pilgrim: from vespers on Saturday to Monday morning no work, no buying or selling, no journey beyond a short limit, no loading; fines in cattle and the forfeit of the goods.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Do not load, sell or set out on a Sunday in an Irish king's land: the goods and the beast or boat that carries them can be taken. The same rule is known to the English.

laws.what: At Scone, on the Hill of Belief, King Constantine and Bishop Cellach swear to keep the laws and discipline of the faith and the rights of the churches and gospels equally with the Gaels.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The church of Alba is one, under a bishop at Saint Andrews (earlier Dunkeld). Its abbots are the men to deal with on that coast.

laws.what: At Chester the kings of the north and west (six by the Chronicle, eight by John of Worcester, among them Kenneth of Alba and Maccus of the Isles) swear to be King Edgar's fellow-workers by sea and land.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A few years in which the Irish Sea has one peace. It ends with Edgar (975); the raids on Cheshire and Anglesey begin again in 980.

laws.what: Mael Sechnaill's proclamation after Tara: every one of the Irish in the Foreigners' land in bondage is to go free to his own land. The annalist calls it the end of Ireland's Babylonian captivity. The Ui Neill are freed of tribute to Dublin from the Shannon to the sea.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Irish slaves cannot be held or sold at Dublin this year, and a buyer who bought last year has lost his money. The trade turns to English, Welsh and Scots captives.

laws.what: The Christmas gold: an ounce of gold from every garth (house-plot) in Dublin to the king of Tara each Christmas night for ever.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A townsman with a plot owes it; so will a foreign merchant who buys one. It shows the town is laid out in plots, each with an owner.

laws.what: The customs of Chester as remembered in 1066: a ship that comes or goes without the king's leave pays forty shillings a man; one that comes against the king's peace is forfeit with crew and cargo; with leave, the king and earl take four pence a load. If the king's reeve orders those with marten skins to sell to none until he has seen them, forty shillings to disobey. Twelve lawmen judge. False measure four shillings; bad ale the dung-stool or four shillings.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Ask leave before the tide takes you up the Dee. Marten skins from Ireland are the king's first choice. The fines are English pence, which the Dublin trade supplies.
laws.source: DB Cheshire 262v (the state of things in 1066; how much older is not known (?))

laws.what: Brian at Armagh lays twenty ounces of gold on the altar and has his clerk write in the Book of Armagh, in his sight, that Armagh's rights over all Ireland are confirmed by the emperor of the Irish.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Armagh's dues run in Munster and at the Norse towns too.

laws.what: Donnchad son of Brian makes a law such as had not been made since Patrick's day: no theft, no feats of arms on Sunday, no going out on Sunday carrying a load, no fetching cattle within doors. In 1050, in a year of bad weather and want, he and the clergy of Munster forbid injustice great and small at Killaloe.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The Sunday rule again, with a king behind it, at Limerick and through Munster.

laws.what: Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, preaches at Bristol against the selling of English men and girls to Ireland, month after month, until the townsmen give it up; King William forbids it later.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The last years of the open slave run from the Severn to Dublin. It was never against the Foreigners' law; it is now against the bishop.
laws.source: William of Malmesbury, Vita Wulfstani ii.20 (the years, about 1062-1080, are not given (?))

laws.what: The thing of the Foreigners: Dublin's assembly mound (the Thingmote) stood east of the town by the Liffey, and Man's at Tynwald. Neither is recorded before the 12th and 13th centuries, but both follow Norse custom.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A dispute between a stranger and a townsman is heard at the thing, where a stranger needs a townsman to speak for him.
laws.source: the mound recorded in Dublin deeds from the 13th century; CM 1228 for Tynwald (?)

coins.what: No coin at all. Cattle, slave women and silver by the ounce in the law tracts; in practice cattle and cloth. A few English and Frankish pennies come as loot: the hoard from Mullaghboden near the Liffey (hidden about 847) is all Frankish deniers of Aquitaine.
coins.source: Kelly, on units of value; num.: Mullaghboden hoard (Dolley 1966 (?))

coins.what: Silver by weight. The Dublin Norse cast ingots and make plain broad arm-rings stamped with punches, cut up as needed (hack-silver); they weigh on small folding scales with lead weights, many of them set with bits of plundered church metalwork. Arabic dirhams reach Ireland by way of York and the Baltic. The hoard from Cuerdale on the Ribble (hidden about 905, some forty kilos) is largely Irish Sea silver of this kind, perhaps the chest of the men driven from Dublin in 902.
coins.source: num.: Sheehan on the Hiberno-Scandinavian arm-rings; Wallace on the Dublin weights; Graham-Campbell, The Cuerdale Hoard (2011)

coins.what: English pennies in Dublin. From Aethelstan's time the Chester mint is among the busiest in England, with many moneyers, and its pennies are the commonest in the Irish hoards. The Dublin kings strike coin at York when they hold it (Sihtric's sword pennies 921-927, Anlaf's raven penny 939-941), never at Dublin.
coins.source: num.: Blunt, Stewart and Lyon, Coinage in Tenth-Century England (1989); Dolley, The Hiberno-Norse Coins in the British Museum (1966)

coins.what: Ring-money in the Isles and Man: plain silver arm-rings made to a rough unit of about 24 grams, with ingots and cut coin. Man is thick with hoards from about 960 to 1070.
coins.source: num.: Graham-Campbell, The Viking-Age Gold and Silver of Scotland (1995); Manx hoards, Bornholdt Collins (?)

coins.what: The first pennies of Dublin, struck for Sihtric Silkbeard from about 995-997: good silver, full weight, close copies of King Aethelred's Crux and then Long Cross, Helmet and Small Cross pennies, reading SIHTRIC REX DYFLIN, some keeping Aethelred's own name. They are taken in England and turn up in Scandinavian hoards.
coins.source: num.: Dolley 1966 (Phase I); Blackburn, Currency under the Vikings, part 4 (2008)

coins.what: Dublin's own Long Cross pennies (Phase II): the one design kept for years, lighter, with pellets added in the quarters. No longer exchanged one for one with English pence; they stay in Ireland and Man.
Pennies struck in Man, copying Dublin's Phase II, cruder and lighter.
coins.source: num.: Dolley, A Hiberno-Manx coinage of the eleventh century (1976); Bornholdt Collins (?)

coins.what: Dublin pennies with a hand in the cross-quarters (Phase III), then with scratched dies (Phase IV, about 1055-1065) and garbled legends (Phase V from about 1065): steadily lighter, baser and harder to read. Good only in Ireland; English pence are still wanted for trade across the sea.
Alba strikes no coin in the whole period (the first Scottish pennies are David I's, 1136). English and Hiberno-Norse pennies and ring-money pass by weight on its coasts.

church.what: Mael Ruain of Tallaght dies: founder (774) of the house at Tallaght, two hours from Duiblinn, head of the Celi De (Culdees), the strict reformers. About 800 Oengus writes his calendar of saints there.
Bresal, abbot of Iona for thirty-one years, dies. About this time the high crosses of Iona and Islay are carved, and, at Iona or Kells, the great Gospel later called the Book of Kells is begun (?).
Kells is given, without a battle, to Columba's community; a new house is built there (807) and its church finished (814), when Abbot Cellach resigns. Iona is not abandoned: monks and an abbot remain.
The martyrdom of Blathmac on Iona.
Abbot Diarmait of Iona goes to Alba with the reliquaries of Colum Cille, and brings them to Ireland in 831.
Feidlimid of Munster seizes Forannan, abbot of Armagh, in the oratory at Kildare: Armagh has two rival abbots for years.

Columba's relics are divided: Abbot Indrechtach brings some to Ireland; Cinaed mac Ailpin carries others to the church he has built, taken to be Dunkeld. Dunkeld is the chief church of the Picts and Scots until Saint Andrews overtakes it about 900.
Indrechtach, abbot of Iona, is killed by English robbers on his way to Rome.
Tuathal son of Artgus, chief bishop of Fortriu and abbot of Dunkeld, dies.
The shrine of Colum Cille and his other relics are brought to Ireland in flight from the Foreigners.

Three Irishmen, Dubslane, Macbeth and Maelinmun, come to King Alfred in a boat of two and a half hides with no oars and food for seven nights, because they wished to be on pilgrimage for the love of God, they cared not where. They land in Cornwall.
Gofraid of Dublin spares the prayer-houses, the Culdees and the sick at Armagh: the first sign of the Foreigners' kings minding the church.
Mael Brigte mac Tornain dies: abbot of Armagh and of Iona together, successor of Patrick and Colum Cille, head of the piety of all Ireland and the greater part of Europe.

On Man, Gaut son of Bjorn carves the first cross-slabs with runes in Norse to Christian dead; one says that Gaut made this and all in Man. Later stones at Andreas and Jurby set Odin and the wolf, and Sigurd roasting the dragon's heart, beside the cross.
church.source: Manx runic crosses: Kirk Michael 101, Andreas 128 (Kermode, Manx Crosses, 1907); dated about 930-1000 by style (?)

church.what: Amlaib Cuaran is baptised in England with King Edmund standing sponsor; Constantine of Alba lays down the kingship and enters the Culdee house at Saint Andrews.
Amlaib Cuaran, king of Dublin for thirty years, goes to Iona in penance and on pilgrimage after the defeat at Tara, and dies there.
The abbot of Iona and fifteen of the elders are killed by Danes on Christmas night.

Olaf Tryggvason, sailing home from the west, forces Earl Sigurd of Orkney to be baptised at Osmundwall, by the saga. Olaf himself is said to have been baptised in the Scilly isles and married in Dublin.
Brian at Armagh confirms its headship over the churches of Ireland.
The theft and finding of the great Gospel of Colum Cille at Kells.
Brian's body is carried from Swords to Armagh by the clergy of Patrick, waked twelve nights and buried in a new tomb.

Sitriuc of Dublin and Flannacan, king of Brega, go to Rome. On his return, about 1030, Sitriuc gives the ground and gold and silver for the church of the Holy Trinity (Christ Church) in Dublin; its first bishop is Dunan (died 1074), whose successor is consecrated at Canterbury.
church.source: AU 1028.7; the Black Book of Christ Church (a later record (?)); AU 1074

church.what: Amlaib son of Sitriuc is killed by English on his way to Rome.

Mac Bethad, king of Alba, at Rome scatters silver to the poor like seed. About the same year Earl Thorfinn of Orkney goes to Rome and builds Christ's church at Birsay, the first bishop's seat in the earldom.
Donnchad son of Brian, put out of his kingdom, dies a pilgrim at Rome in the monastery of Saint Stephen; Echmarcach, once king of Dublin and Man, dies there the next year.

trade_notes.what: What Dublin sells: slaves above all (Irish to 980, then English, Welsh and Scots); hides and wool cloaks from the Irish kings; marten, otter and other skins; ships and crews for hire. What it buys: wine and salt from Francia, English silver pennies and pottery, walrus ivory, amber and soapstone from the north, jet from Whitby, silk.
trade_notes.source: the Dublin excavations at Wood Quay and Fishamble Street (Wallace, Viking Dublin: The Wood Quay Excavations, 2016); DB Cheshire for the marten skins

trade_notes.what: The great longship found at Roskilde (Skuldelev 2, thirty metres, sixty oars or more) was built of oak felled in the Dublin region in 1042.
trade_notes.source: dendrochronology, Viking Ship Museum Roskilde (Crumlin-Pedersen and Olsen 2002)

trade_notes.what: Findan, a Leinster man, was sold to Northmen about 845, passed from ship to ship, escaped on Orkney by hiding under a rock in the tide, and ended a hermit at Rheinau on the Rhine (died 878).

The Fragmentary Annals tell that the sons of the king of Laithlind brought a host of Moorish captives, 'blue men', from the raid on Spain and Mauretania (859-861) to Ireland, where they long remained.
The game has no port for Man, the Wirral shore, Waterford (from 914), Limerick (from 922), Wexford or Cork, nor for Dumbarton, Dunkeld or Whithorn. This file names them in words.
